newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries close off, supply weighs on prices.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries close off, supply weighs on prices.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed lower for the third consecutive session as recent heavy supply and bearish market psychology took an expensive toll on government debt securities on Friday, analysts said.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended down 12/32 at 95-3/32. Its yield rose 6.89 percent against 6.86 percent in the previous day.
"We're looking at the same thing that has been a problem for some time, which is supply," said John Canavan, a market analyst at Stone and McCarthy Research Associates Inc.

"In addition to that, the market is still trying to digest the two-year and the five-year note auctions ... And also the psychology, the market just remains terribly bearish. There isn't a lot of buyers out there," Canavan added.
Traders said the distribution of the two-year and the five-year note sales held earlier this week was difficult.

Players who went long and purchased the securities at the auctions were said to be facing losses after the market's recent downturn. That has prompted many of them to dump securities in the cash market, which in turn has fueled the bearish sentiment even further, traders added.
"There was strong activity in the new two and five-year notes today ... A lot of people were trying to unload them," said a trader at a foreign investment bank here.
Analysts said continued heavy issuance of corporate debt and mortage-backed securities weighed on prices as well. "We took in even more corporate supply today," the trader said.
Pundits said a drop in the stock market also contributed to fuel the bearish sentiment. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped for the second day in a row to close down 59 points at 6,696.48.
The market staged a small reaction during the mid-afternoon session when traders reported rumors of some foreign central bank buying in the long end of the curve.
Treasuries pared some losses, but the market's strength was not enough to put prices back into black.

Although no major economic indicator was announced on Friday, analysts said participants remained wary of the possibility of higher-than-expected growth in the fourth quarter of 1996 as well as in the first quarter of 1997.
"It certainly looks like the market has reacted to the (economic) strength in the fourth quarter," said David Hensley, economist at Salomon Brothers.
Hensley said he was expecting fourth quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth slightly above four percent and final sales growth above five percent.
"Those are very strong numbers," Hensley said.

Analysts expect upcoming key data will provide some direction to the market. The highlights of the week include the employment cost index on Tuesday and GDP data on Friday. Both indicators are for the fourth quarter of 1996.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed flat at 5.03 percent. The six-month bill rate rose one basis point to 5.13 percent. The year bill rate was unchanged at 5.30 percent.

The two-year note closed down 1/32 at 99-21/32, yielding 6.06 percent. The five-year note traded off 4/32 at 99-13/32 to yield 6.39 percent. The ten-year note closed down 8/32 at 99-3/32, yielding 6.63 percent.
